---
title: "Government spending multipliers"
subtitle: "Ramey and Zubairy (2018), linear model: US quarterly data, 1889Q1–2015Q4"
engine: julia
---

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
include("_setup.jl")
```

Ramey and Zubairy (2018, *JPE*) estimate how much GDP rises when government
spending rises, using more than a century of US quarterly data. This page
replicates the baseline linear model from their Stata program `jordagk.do`:
the impulse responses, the one-step cumulative multiplier, the two-step
multiplier and the weak-instrument diagnostic. The authors build every lead,
cumulated sum and lag by hand and loop `ivreg2` over horizons. Here each is a
single call.

## Data and specification

The cleaned dataset ships with the package as
`docs/src/data/ramey_zubairy.csv`, built from the replication package with the
variable definitions of `jordagk.do`. GDP and spending are divided by
potential GDP (the Gordon–Krenn normalization), so regression coefficients are
already in dollars of GDP per dollar of spending.

```{julia}
rz = rz_data()
first(rz[:, [:quarter, :y, :g, :newsy, :unemp]], 3)
```

Two shocks identify spending changes:

| Shock | Instrument $s_t$ | Controls $w_{t-1}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Military news | `newsy`: news about future military spending, over lagged potential GDP | 4 lags of `newsy`, `y`, `g` |
| Blanchard–Perotti | `bp`: current spending, taken as predetermined | 4 lags of `y`, `g` |

`newsy` starts in 1890Q1: the file begins in 1889Q1, and its first lag does
not exist.

## Impulse responses

The responses of spending and GDP at horizon $h$ are the coefficients on the
shock in $x_{t+h} = \alpha_h + \beta_h s_t + \gamma_h' w_{t-1} + u_{t+h}$.
`leads(x)` puts $x_{t+h}$ on the left and `lp` runs the regression for every
$h$ up to `horizon`:

```{julia}
irf_y_news = lp(@formula(leads(y) ~ newsy + lags(newsy, 4) + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)),
    rz; horizon = 20)
irf_g_news = lp(@formula(leads(g) ~ newsy + lags(newsy, 4) + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)),
    rz; horizon = 20)
irf_y_bp = lp(@formula(leads(y) ~ bp + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)), rz; horizon = 20)
irf_g_bp = lp(@formula(leads(g) ~ bp + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)), rz; horizon = 20)

hac = Bartlett{NeweyWest}()      # Newey–West, automatic bandwidth
summarize(irf_y_news, hac; term = :newsy, level = 0.90)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Responses of government spending and GDP. 90% bands, Newey–West automatic bandwidth."
s_irf = (g_news = summarize(irf_g_news, hac; term = :newsy, level = 0.90),
    g_bp = summarize(irf_g_bp, hac; term = :bp, level = 0.90),
    y_news = summarize(irf_y_news, hac; term = :newsy, level = 0.90),
    y_bp = summarize(irf_y_bp, hac; term = :bp, level = 0.90))
plot(irfpanel(s_irf.g_news; title = "Government spending · news"),
    irfpanel(s_irf.g_bp; title = "Government spending · Blanchard–Perotti"),
    irfpanel(s_irf.y_news; title = "GDP · news", xlab = "quarters"),
    irfpanel(s_irf.y_bp; title = "GDP · Blanchard–Perotti", xlab = "quarters");
    layout = (2, 2), size = (900, 560), FIGKW...)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
peak(s) = (i = argmax(s.coef); (h = s.horizon[i], b = s.coef[i]))
pk_y, pk_g, pk_gbp = peak(s_irf.y_news), peak(s_irf.g_news), peak(s_irf.g_bp)
```

After a news shock both responses are hump-shaped: spending peaks at
`{julia} f2(pk_g.b)` after `{julia} pk_g.h` quarters, GDP at
`{julia} f2(pk_y.b)` after `{julia} pk_y.h`. Under Blanchard–Perotti the shock
*is* current spending, so spending moves one for one on impact, keeps rising
to `{julia} f2(pk_gbp.b)` after `{julia} pk_gbp.h` quarters, then declines.

## The one-step cumulative multiplier

The multiplier at horizon $h$ is cumulative extra GDP per cumulative extra
dollar of spending. Ramey and Zubairy estimate it in one step, as $m_h$ in

$$
\sum_{j=0}^{h} y_{t+j} = \alpha_h + m_h \sum_{j=0}^{h} g_{t+j} + \gamma_h' w_{t-1} + u_{t+h},
$$

with cumulative spending instrumented by the shock $s_t$. Both sides move with
the horizon, and `cumul` handles either side, so `lpiv` returns the whole
multiplier path at once:

```{julia}
mult_news = lpiv(TSLS(), @formula(cumul(y) ~ (cumul(g) ~ newsy) +
                                  lags(newsy, 4) + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)), rz; horizon = 20)
mult_bp = lpiv(TSLS(), @formula(cumul(y) ~ (cumul(g) ~ bp) + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)),
    rz; horizon = 20)

s_news = summarize(mult_news, hac; level = 0.90)   # the multiplier is `shock`, no `term`
s_bp = summarize(mult_bp, hac; level = 0.90)
nobs(mult_bp)[[1, 9, 21]]                          # h = 0, 8, 20: Stata's samples
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "One-step cumulative multipliers. 90% bands, Newey–West automatic bandwidth; the dotted line is a multiplier of one."
plot(irfpanel(s_news; title = "Cumulative multiplier · news", reference = 1.0,
        xlab = "quarters"),
    irfpanel(s_bp; title = "Cumulative multiplier · Blanchard–Perotti",
        reference = 1.0, xlab = "quarters");
    layout = (1, 2), size = (900, 300), FIGKW...)
```

::: {.lead-in}
The two-year multiplier is **`{julia} f2(s_news.coef[9])`** for the news shock
and **`{julia} f2(s_bp.coef[9])`** for Blanchard–Perotti. Both are below one,
the paper's headline result.
:::

### Against the published numbers

`RZ` is the authors' published multiplier from
`Multiplier-Standard-Errors.xlsx` in the replication package. Horizons 8 and 16
are the two-year and four-year multipliers in the paper.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
P = RZ_PUBLISHED
ix = P.h .+ 1
mdtable(["h", "news", "s.e.", "RZ", "RZ s.e.", "BP", "s.e.", "RZ", "RZ s.e."],
    [[string(P.h[k]), f3(s_news.coef[ix[k]]), f3(s_news.se[ix[k]]), f3(P.news[k]),
        f3(P.news_se[k]), f3(s_bp.coef[ix[k]]), f3(s_bp.se[ix[k]]), f3(P.bp[k]),
        f3(P.bp_se[k])] for k in eachindex(P.h)])
gap = vcat(abs.(s_news.coef[ix] .- P.news) ./ P.news_se,
    abs.(s_bp.coef[ix] .- P.bp) ./ P.bp_se)
se_ratio = vcat(s_news.se[ix] ./ P.news_se, s_bp.se[ix] ./ P.bp_se)
nothing
```

At these `{julia} length(P.h)` horizons, for both shocks, every point estimate
is within `{julia} f2(maximum(gap))` published standard errors of the
authors' value, with a median gap of `{julia} f2(median(gap))`. The remaining
difference is most likely the data vintage: the spreadsheet of published
numbers predates the last revision of the shipped data by a week.

The standard errors differ more, `{julia} f2(minimum(se_ratio))` to
`{julia} f2(maximum(se_ratio))` times the published ones, for two reasons:

- **Bandwidth.** The paper uses `ivreg2, robust bw(auto)`. Both sides implement
  the Newey–West (1994) automatic rule, but they select different bandwidths on
  the same regression. With a fixed bandwidth, `Bartlett(b)` here and `bw(b)`
  in Stata, coefficients and IV standard errors agree to about $10^{-10}$.
- **Degrees of freedom.** `ivreg2` applies no small-sample factor. The
  standard errors here, IV and OLS alike, carry $n/(n-k)$ and are 1–3% larger
  than Stata's `ivreg2` equivalents.

## The two-step multiplier

The paper's alternative estimator is the ratio of the cumulative sums of the
two impulse responses, $\sum_{j \le h} \hat\beta^y_j \,/\, \sum_{j \le h} \hat\beta^g_j$:

```{julia}
twostep(ry, rg, shock) = cumsum(coefpath(ry; term = shock)) ./
                         cumsum(coefpath(rg; term = shock))
two_news = twostep(irf_y_news, irf_g_news, :newsy)
two_bp = twostep(irf_y_bp, irf_g_bp, :bp)
(news = maximum(abs.(two_news .- s_news.coef)), bp = maximum(abs.(two_bp .- s_bp.coef)))
```

The two estimators agree to within `{julia} f4(maximum(abs.(two_news .- s_news.coef)))`
(news) and `{julia} f4(maximum(abs.(two_bp .- s_bp.coef)))` (Blanchard–Perotti)
at every horizon, because here the one-step regressions use the same sample as
the impulse-response regressions. Ramey and Zubairy note that the two can
diverge in other specifications, precisely when the samples differ.

## Is the instrument strong enough?

A multiplier estimated with a weak instrument is biased and its bands
undercover. `weakivtest` computes the Montiel Olea–Pflueger effective *F* at
each horizon, from the HAC covariance attached to the model:

```{julia}
w_news = weakivtest(mult_news + vcov(hac))         # one test per horizon
w_bp = weakivtest(mult_bp + vcov(hac))
w_news[9]                                          # two years out
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Montiel Olea–Pflueger effective F, log scale. The dashed line is the 5% critical value for a worst-case bias of 10%."
F_eff(ws) = [w === nothing ? NaN : w.F_eff for w in ws]
F_news, F_bp = F_eff(w_news), F_eff(w_bp)
cv = w_news[1].cv_TSLS[2]
plot(fpanel(0:20, F_news, cv; title = "Effective F · news", xlab = "quarters"),
    fpanel(0:20, F_bp, cv; title = "Effective F · Blanchard–Perotti",
        labelpos = :bottom, xlab = "quarters");
    layout = (1, 2), size = (900, 300), FIGKW...)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
hpk = argmax(F_news) - 1
weak_from = findfirst(h -> all(F_bp[(h + 1):end] .< cv), 1:20)
```

The news instrument never clears the critical value of
`{julia} f2(cv)`: its effective *F* peaks at `{julia} f2(F_news[hpk + 1])` at
`{julia} hpk` quarters. Blanchard–Perotti is strong at short horizons and falls
below the threshold from horizon `{julia} weak_from` on. At $h = 0$ its
instrument *is* the regressor: the regression treats it as exogenous, there is
no first stage to test (`weakivtest` returns `nothing`), and the figure omits
that point. Ramey and Zubairy respond to weak instruments with
Anderson–Rubin inference, which the package does not implement yet.

## Bias correction and bootstrap bands

The bands above use Newey–West standard errors. Montiel Olea, Plagborg-Møller,
Qian and Wolf (2025) recommend a different recipe for local projections:
correct the estimates for small-sample bias with the procedure of Herbst and
Johannsen (2024), and report either heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors or,
better, the bands of a VAR moving-block bootstrap. The bootstrap fits a VAR to
the data, its slopes corrected for bias with Pope's (1990) formula, resamples its
residuals in overlapping blocks, re-estimates the complete local projection on
each artificial sample, and builds Hall percentile-$t$ bands. `biascorrect` and
`varbootstrap` implement it, with both corrections on by default. The procedure
is for OLS projections, so it covers the impulse responses but not the IV
multiplier.

The VAR is fitted on the shock and the two responses, which must have no
missing values, so the first quarters, before `newsy` starts, are dropped. The
estimation samples do not change. The reference picks the lag order by AIC and
uses it for both the projection's controls and the bootstrap VAR:

```{julia}
using Random: Xoshiro
rzc = dropmissing(rz, [:newsy, :y, :g])
sel = lagselect(rzc, [:newsy, :y, :g]; maxlags = 10, criterion = :aic)
nlags(sel)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
bic_p = argmin(sel.bic)
```

AIC picks `{julia} nlags(sel)` lags (BIC would pick `{julia} bic_p`). Both the
four lags of the Ramey–Zubairy specification and the AIC order are shown below.
`@formula` takes a literal lag count, so each order is written out:

```{julia}
boot(f, p) = varbootstrap(lp(f, rzc; horizon = 20), rzc; vars = [:newsy, :y, :g],
                          nlags = p, nboot = 1000, rng = Xoshiro(20260916))
# the same seed gives both responses the same artificial samples
b4 = (y = boot(@formula(leads(y) ~ newsy + lags(newsy, 4) + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)), 4),
      g = boot(@formula(leads(g) ~ newsy + lags(newsy, 4) + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)), 4))
b9 = (y = boot(@formula(leads(y) ~ newsy + lags(newsy, 9) + lags(y, 9) + lags(g, 9)), 9),
      g = boot(@formula(leads(g) ~ newsy + lags(newsy, 9) + lags(y, 9) + lags(g, 9)), 9))
summarize(b4.y; level = 0.90)       # bias-corrected path, Hall percentile-t band
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Responses to the news shock: Herbst–Johannsen bias-corrected local projection (solid) with 68% and 90% Hall percentile-t bands from the VAR moving-block bootstrap (1000 draws, Pope-corrected VAR); the uncorrected OLS path is dashed."
# the uncorrected OLS path: `b.lp` wraps it when the bias correction is on
olspath(b) = coefpath(b.lp isa BiasCorrectedLP ? b.lp.lp : b.lp; term = :newsy)
function bootpanel(b; title, xlab = "")
    s90, s68 = summarize(b; level = 0.90), summarize(b; level = 0.68)
    H = s90.horizon
    p = plot(H, s90.lower; fillrange = s90.upper, linealpha = 0, fillcolor = INK,
             fillalpha = 0.12, title, xlabel = xlab, base()...)
    plot!(p, H, s68.lower; fillrange = s68.upper, linealpha = 0, fillcolor = INK,
          fillalpha = 0.2)
    hline!(p, [0.0]; c = RULE, ls = :dot, lw = 0.8)
    plot!(p, H, olspath(b); c = INK, ls = :dash, lw = 1.0)
    plot!(p, H, s90.coef; c = INK, lw = 1.8)
    return p
end
plot(bootpanel(b4.g; title = "Government spending · 4 lags (RZ)"),
     bootpanel(b4.y; title = "GDP · 4 lags (RZ)"),
     bootpanel(b9.g; title = "Government spending · $(nlags(sel)) lags (AIC)", xlab = "quarters"),
     bootpanel(b9.y; title = "GDP · $(nlags(sel)) lags (AIC)", xlab = "quarters");
     layout = (2, 2), size = (900, 560), FIGKW...)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
bpeak(b) = (s = summarize(b; level = 0.9); i = argmax(s.coef); (h = s.horizon[i], b = s.coef[i]))
excl(b) = (s = summarize(b; level = 0.9); findall((s.lower .> 0) .| (s.upper .< 0)) .- 1)
# horizons as runs: [0, 1, 2, 18] -> "0–2 and 18"
function span(v)
    isempty(v) && return "none"
    runs = UnitRange{Int}[]
    for h in v
        !isempty(runs) && h == last(runs[end]) + 1 ? (runs[end] = first(runs[end]):h) :
            push!(runs, h:h)
    end
    parts = [length(r) == 1 ? string(first(r)) : "$(first(r))–$(last(r))" for r in runs]
    return length(parts) == 1 ? parts[1] : join(parts[1:(end - 1)], ", ") * " and " * parts[end]
end
shift(b) = maximum(abs.(summarize(b; level = 0.9).coef .- olspath(b)))
nfail = sum(b.nfail for b in (b4..., b9...))
pope = unique([b.pope_delta for b in (b4..., b9...)])
p4y, p4g, p9y, p9g = bpeak(b4.y), bpeak(b4.g), bpeak(b9.y), bpeak(b9.g)
```

With four lags, GDP peaks at `{julia} f2(p4y.b)` after `{julia} p4y.h` quarters
and spending at `{julia} f2(p4g.b)` after `{julia} p4g.h`. On this long sample
the bias correction moves the paths by at most
`{julia} f3(max(shift(b4.y), shift(b4.g)))`. The 90% band excludes zero at
horizons `{julia} span(excl(b4.y))` for GDP and `{julia} span(excl(b4.g))` for
spending. With `{julia} nlags(sel)` lags the shape is the same (peaks of
`{julia} f2(p9y.b)` for GDP at `{julia} p9y.h` quarters and `{julia} f2(p9g.b)`
for spending at `{julia} p9g.h`), but the bands are wider at long horizons and
right-skewed: they exclude zero at horizons `{julia} span(excl(b9.y))` for GDP
and `{julia} span(excl(b9.g))` for spending. Bands are pointwise, and because
the percentile-$t$ construction corrects for bias they need not be centred on
the estimate. `{julia} nfail` of the 4000 draws fail, and the Pope correction
applies `{julia} pope == [1.0] ? "in full in all four bootstraps" : "partially (pope_delta = $(pope))"`.
